source_excerpts.text:
The chosen opening: quantum prediction from conditional samples

I developed a general way to use an acquired conditional sampler directly for quantum prediction. The strongest result is a theorem: for a state with known phases, prefix-conditional samples suffice to estimate efficiently described sparse quantum observables with essentially the usual inverse-square Monte Carlo accuracy dependence, while charging the conditional computation.

The key construction is an importance-sampling estimator whose correction variance decreases with the squared amplitude error. That makes increasingly accurate—and increasingly expensive—conditional approximations useful without paying their full cost on every observable sample.

This gives the existing machinery a broader purpose. It can supply nonlocal coherent observables, reduced-state moments, conditional-model comparisons, and some entanglement witnesses through classical computation. The clean coherent interface remains available for outputs that require a quantum state or coherent composition.

I completed a finite implementation that certifies entanglement of its specified pure state at 95% conditional confidence. The constants are substantial: it consumed 931,905,440 conditional draws, and direct computation wins decisively on that small input. The earned advance is the reusable theorem and its verified output interface; a broad practical advantage remains unestablished.

The complete result is preserved in 
MAIN_RESULT.md

This is an informed coordinator assessment with prior exposure. The ordinary manuscript/program bytes were not newly acquired or replayed. A native worker explicitly reports checking the sparse-observable theorem, finite schedule and confidence amplification, finding no substantive failure and correcting power-of-two row-slot sampling plus the small-error range of the lower bound. That internal review counts at its reported scope; it is not a blind coordinator reconstruction or proof of every implementation and comparison. Exact worker briefs, history isolation and total costs are unobserved.

The main advance is the variance bridge, rather than another scalar expectation formula. Two normalized approximate amplitude vectors admit a sampleable four-way proposal for the difference of monomial expectations. The correction is unbiased for that difference, bounded in magnitude and has second moment at most four times squared amplitude distance. The parent extends it to sparse Hermitian rows with bound `4 d A^2 ||a-b||^2`. It avoids a minimum-probability or bounded-amplitude-ratio promise. A consistent cached surrogate must be retained inside a replicate; independent estimator replicates get fresh trees and independent output words. Resampling every amplitude or using predictor randomness to select outputs breaks the argument. The supplied phase must be efficiently computable; probabilities alone do not reveal it.

The add-one conditional estimator supplies forward-KL and squared-amplitude-error control. A geometric hierarchy makes correction variance decrease as `2^-ell`. The complete receiver bound is proportional to `epsilon^-2 (sum sqrt(V_ell W_ell))^2`, plus ceiling work and confidence amplification. Only under justified uniform conditional setup/draw bounds does the advertised near-inverse-square expression follow. Physical mesh, retained-mode lattice, center acquisition, rejection and finite arithmetic remain inside the actual source costs, potentially adding accuracy powers. This is not a general efficient quantum simulator or an inverse-square theorem for the entire physical computation.
